items.body:
Oren Ambarchi's kraut-techno-free jazz magnum opus is back for its 10th anniversary -  an ambitious ensemble piece featuring an all-star list of players including Ricardo Villalobos, Keith Fullerton Whitman, Mark Fell, crys Cole, Will Guthrie, Arto Lindsay and Konrad Sprenger... Wooooo

You've got to admire Ambarchi's chutzpah here. 'Hubris' is an all you can eat buffet of his various musical cravings, a chance for his friends, influences and collaborators to flex a little and for Ambarchi to attempt to ride the groove like an experienced cowboy on an out-of-control bucking bronco. The first side is the biggest surprise, a dedication to Wang Chung's enduring, disco-influenced 'To Live and Die in L.A.' soundtrack that begins with ping-ponging guitar notes and Jim O'Rourke's synth blips, before elusive Berlin-based composer Konrad Sprenger (aka Joerg Hiller) drops in with some motorized guitar vamps. It's rhythmic gear that fits in with the Berlin school until Mark Fell appears in the final third with some typically fractured percussion.

On the flip, the groove loosens after a short guitar interlude. Ricardo Villalobos takes over with a suitably winding, minimal throb over live rhythms played by Joe Talia and Will Guthrie simultaneously as krautrock techno mutates into disco fusion. Keith Fullerton Whitman tries to nudge the track off the rails with his modular expositions, but the path is set - Arto Lindsay's axe is just the icing on the cake. By the end of the side, we're in full jazz-noise mode: everything's still pegged to Villalobos' central pulse, but that's the only element that's bolted down. 

Hard to believe it's 10 years already - we can't think of a better skeleton key to unlock the secrets behind Black Truffle's musical identity.
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是Ambarchi的集大成之作，汇聚了多位不同领域的音乐家展开合作。第一面以吉他音符与合成器碎片开始，融入机动化吉他循环与碎裂化打击乐，将柏林学派节奏逻辑与自由即兴交织。第二面节奏进一步松散，Villalobos的极简脉冲成为锚点，鼓手与模块合成器在此基础上展开多重对话，最终滑入爵士与噪音的混合状态。整张作品展示了协作者各自的美学取向如何在同一框架内共存，既是集体创作也是个人表达的载体。作为独立厂牌Black Truffle的代表作之一，它展现了实验音乐跨领域协作的多种可能性。

items.body:
16 hours of peerless, important works by Eliane Radigue relating to her work with the ARP 2500 synthesiser between 1971-2000. Prior to this period, Eliane worked exclusively with feedback on tape and oscillators, but her work from the ‘70s onward is defined by an uniquely meditative and transcendent grasp of microtonal minimalism which has latterly come to place her among the 20th century’s most esteemed and truly inimitable composers. Bearing in mind that Eliane realised this fathomless body of work in her Paris apartment away from professional recording studios, only makes it resonate more strongly with the idea that Eliane was a genuine outlier whose uniquely sober work divined an unquantifiable yet ultimately human nature in electronic music. RIP legend.

"Eliane Radigue was born in Paris. She studied “musique concrète” techniques at the “Studio d’Essai” of the RTF under the direction of Pierre Schaeffer and Pierre Henry (1956-57). She was married to the painter and sculptor Arman and devoted ten years to their three children. She then worked with Pierre Henry, as his assistant at the Studio APSOME (1967-68). She was in residence at the New York University School of Arts (1970-71), the University of Iowa and the California Institute of the Arts (1973) and Mills College (1998). She has created sound environments using looped tapes of various durations, gradually desynchronising.

Her works have been featured in numerous galleries and museums since the late 60s and from 1970, she has been associated to the ARP 2500 Synthesizer and tape through many compositions from Chry-ptus (1970) up to L’Île resonante (2000). These include: Biogenesis, Arthesis, Ψ 847, Adnos I, II and III (70s), Les Chants de Milarepa and Jetsun Mila (80s) and the three pieces constituting the Trilogie de la Mort (1988-91-93). Since 2002, she has been composing mostly acoustic works for performers and instruments. Her music has been featured in major international festivals. Her extremely sober, almost ascetic concerts, are made of a continuous, ever-changing yet extremely slow stream of sound, whose transformation occurs within the sonic material itself.

Radigue found her musical voice through the decisive encounter with “musique concrète” and its founding fathers. With Pierre Schaeffer, first, and then Pierre Henry, with whom she learned and perfected the art of tape recorders. She then developed a unique style by herself, freely continuing the exploration of electronic sounds, progressing with tenacity through her musical quest, without worrying about current trends or fashions, paying no attention to creeds or dogmas. An isolated course, out with fashions and institutions, such a singular and intense music, so remote from everything..."
items._genre: experimental electronic / drone / minimalist / synthesizer music
items._cn_summary: 这张合辑收录了Eliane Radigue在1971至2000年间使用ARP 2500合成器创作的电子作品，总时长16小时。她早期专注于磁带反馈与振荡器，70年代后转向微观调式极简主义，音色呈现冥想性与超越性的特质。所有作品均在她巴黎公寓中完成，远离专业录音室，强化了她作为独立于体制之外创作者的形象。评论将她的音乐描述为缓慢、连续、不断变化的声流，其变化发生在声音材料内部，具有几乎禁欲式的克制。从早期Chry-ptus到L'Île resonante，再到三联作Trilogie de la Mort，她延续了Pierre Schaeffer与Pierre Henry开创的具体音乐传统，发展出独树一帜的个人语言，对20世纪电子音乐史具有重要意义。

items.body:
Epic 16 hour François Bayle retrospective, an unparalleled document of the key C.20th electro-acoustic and concrète pioneer and director of the hugely influential GRM institution from 1966-1997, where he was instrumental in bringing the Acousmonium speaker array and INA-GRM label to life, among many important, enduring innovations

This 10 year reissue of ’50 Ans d’Acousmagique’ joins INA-GRM’s quintessential boxsets of Pierre Schaeffer, Pierre Henry, Parmegiani, Radigue, and Xenakis in a rare, stellar microcosm of works by twentieth century groundbreakers. At 16 hrs long, and including 228 tracks, it offers a comprehensive overview of François Bayle’s unfathomable catalogue of work between 1972-2012. During this time Bayle was pivotal in altering perceptions of music’s materiality and purpose at the most fundamental and philosophic levels through his work in developing the Acousmonium diffusion system - an “orchestra of loudspeakers” which has become key to the GRM’s facilities in Paris - as well as supporting technological developments (Syter, GRM Tools, Midi Formers, Acousmographe) which are vital to his own remarkable compositions, and his endeavours organising radio broadcasts and events. 

Deeply informing and paralleling the history of recorded electronic music during its formative golden years, Bayle’s recordings render an embarrassment of riches for the discerning and explorative listener and historians of vanguard C.20th music. Between the flighty electro-acoustic staging of his avian dreams on ’72’s ‘Trois Rêves D'oiseau’ to the sensually lathered cosmic delirium of 1978-80’s ‘Erosphère’ works, to his beguiling latter tributes to his tutors at the Paris Conservatoire and Darmstadt summer courses, Messiaen and Stockhausen; the overwhelming scope of Bayle’s work, and thus the boxset, is brought into clearer focus by its chronological sequencing, offering a logical pathway thru his incredible projections of imagination.

It bears reflection that figures such as François Bayle created, and then opened, doors of perception for music in the past century that have come to mirror and shape the soundsphere we now inhabit. His innovations in sound spatialisation and the embrace of an acoustic unknown, or acousmagique, underline some of the most fascinating expressions of pathos thru art in our lifetimes, and this boxset is more than enough to send heads reeling into deep time for eons to come.
items._genre: electro-acoustic / acousmatic / concrète / sound spatialisation / experimental electronic
items._cn_summary: 这套15CD盒装精选收录了法国电声与具体音乐先驱弗朗索瓦·拜勒跨越1972至2012年间的作品，总时长约16小时、含228首曲目，按编年时间顺序编排。拜勒长期担任巴黎GRM研究所所长（1966-1997），是Acousmonium扬声器阵列系统的核心开发者，该系统将声音空间化作为音乐创作与扩散的核心手段；同时他推动了Syter、GRM Tools、Acousmographe等软硬件工具的发展。盒装作品风格跨度极大：从1972年以鸟类鸣叫为灵感的早期电声剧场，到1978-80年代带有宇宙感性与感官迷醉的'Erosphère'系列，再到晚期向梅西安与施托克豪森致敬的篇章。其作品不仅是二十世纪后半叶录音电子音乐史的平行文献，也系统性地拓宽了音乐的物质性与空间性概念。该选集与INA-GRM此前发行的谢费尔、亨利、帕尔梅贾尼、拉迪格、泽纳基斯等大师盒装共同构成完整的二十世纪先锋音乐档案。

items.body:
12th Isle push the boat out to Rosso Polare’s uchronic folklore, pulling from the Milanese artist’s Italian folk heritage and weaving in chops by Persian electro-acoustic artist Cinna Peyghamy, plus Italian avant-garde veteran Riccardo Sinigaglia, for an adventurous session braiding folk and concrète timelines... 

“Cacciamali is an exploration of diegetic sound, folk chants and traditional rhythms and instrumentation building upon Milan based Rosso Polare’s last outing Campo Amaro and the subsequent departure of co-founder Anna Vezzosi from the group. Where the 2024 album incorporated a heavy use of folklore as a new tool, Cacciamali explores the influence further by bringing in a host of collaborative players including Italian avant-garde veteran Riccardo Sinigaglia, sound artist and researcher HMOT (Stas Shärifulla) and Persian/Parisian electro-acoustic musician Cinna Peyghamy.

‘Scoff Back Sickness’, as the title loosely translates, utilises the same approach, one based on non-hierarchical authorship and leaning heavily on field recordings that both contrast and blend with the tonal material, focusing on biophony, landscape and environmental audio as compositional material. Shifting closer now to a shared network of voices and materials, the dual narrative unfolds as such:

Side A is connected to the concept of the medieval quintain games, specifically flag throwing, where certain drumming patterns from the tradition have been overworked, distorted and transformed. Side B is an underlying local legend from the north of Italy, where some sources speak of a presumed duel in 1744 between a father and his son, ultimately ending with the son’s death. These two layers are not illustrative but structural: ritual / repetition / tradition on one side, and rupture / conflict / loss on the other. A struggle to keep floating, a long shout in the distance, suspended between memory, ritual and disappearance. The result is dense, thick with impulse yet also measured, and often leaves us disoriented and questioning a sound's origin the moment we think we have a grip on the process. The gentle nostalgia of close-mic’ed ‘Falò’ summons the spirit of René Aubry & Jean Schwarz’s concréte masterpiece ‘Five Women’ on the Still Waters ballet soundtrack, and the stark contrast of looping rhythms on both ‘Xiv - Pavo’ and ‘Monte’ deploys a driving, intentful break from the moments of worldly human interactions served by the field recordings.”
items._genre: experimental / electroacoustic / folk concrète / field recording
items._cn_summary: Rosso Polare 延续前作对民间传说的挖掘，带来新作《Cacciamali》。专辑以米兰艺术家的意大利民间传统为根基，融入波斯电声艺术家 Cinna Peyghamy、意大利先锋老将 Riccardo Sinigaglia 及声音研究者 HMOT 的协作，形成跨越民间音乐与具体音乐（concrète）的时间线交织。整体采用去中心化的创作方式，大量运用田野录音与生物声学素材，与器乐声部形成既对比又融合的层次关系。A 面取材于中世纪枪旗游戏的鼓点节奏，经变形处理后构成仪式/重复/传统的结构维度；B 面则以北意大利1744年父子决斗的传说为底层叙事，呈现断裂/冲突/丧失的面向。两种叙事不作为装饰而是结构性存在，悬浮于记忆、仪式与消逝之间。作品密度高、充满冲动却保持克制，听者常在自以为抓住其逻辑时再度迷失方向。

items.body:
On a label full of weirdos, outliers, mavericks and freaks, clandestine Greek anomaly Aeson Zervas is Heat Crimes’ OG wildcard, landing a debut album a couple of years ago that sounded like The Caretaker channeling crates of rebetika, and now returning with this deeply elusive new LP of plasmic synths that unfolds in ways that will leave you with a proper motion sickness of time travel. Aye, it’s a special one.

After lighting up 2024 with blink ’n miss LP & tape drops, Aeson Zervas’s 3rd instalment dips into a perpetual night world of cobwebbed keyboard melodies and flame flicker incantations designed to score your next regression session. As ever, the label and artist remain tight-lipped about pretty much everything, but the vibe is self-evidently clammy and febrile thru a dozen parts familiar to both preceding drops, woven between pillars of inspiration in lemniscate loops and free flowing rhythmelodic arrangements that bind his ideas to bezonked minds.

The Mesolonghi-based enigma continues to prove a master of hypnosis and a conduit for ancient spirits seeping into the modern world, luring susceptible minds to states of bliss and dread, but not without that sense of romance that also lit up his prior releases. Once again feeling the same pull of past worlds as The Caretaker, only slanted to microtonal scales, his mix of lopped-off and extended melodies tell arcane stories still salient to contemporary imaginations able to tune in.

Activating with a section of meditative, almost no-wave strafing discord, themes of shimmering exotica slide into backyard ritualism, with a lilting marimba sounding like it escaped a Martin Denny side before bleeding into a Giallo-esque wheeze, thru port and island-hopping rebetika, and properly haunting passages of midnight sacred music swarmed by cicadas. The 6th (Χωρίς τίτλο 23) part of needling Italianate arps and screeches is particularly affective, as is the plugged-in folkdance sputter of the 8th (Χωρίς τίτλο 25), and a final couplet coming off like Muslimgauze with a thing for sleazy horror, not dub.

Basically, whatever this label serve, lap it up while you can.
items._genre: experimental electronic / dark ambient / world fusion / microtonal
items._cn_summary: 希腊独立厂牌Heat Crimes旗下艺术家Aeson Zervas的第三张专辑，以密织的键盘旋律与火焰般的吟唱构建出一座永恒的暗夜世界。整张作品游走于微观调律体系之中，将rebetika（希腊传统民间音乐）的古老灵韵、Martin Denny式的异域声响、Giallo电影配乐的诡异气韵以及Muslimgauze式的政治化暗流编织在一起。十二个段落如同不断折叠的无限符号，循环往复却拒绝重复，每一段都暗示着不同仪式场景——冥想式的近无浪潮切割、院落中的秘密仪式、半夜被蝉鸣包围的圣咏。专辑在催眠般的恍惚与浪漫之间取得平衡，合成器质感黏腻而发热，旋律被裁断或拉长，似在讲述只有当代敏感心灵才能破译的隐秘叙事。作为来自希腊Mesolonghi的独立制作，在风格融合深度、文化独特性与实验性三个维度上均展现出罕见的完整性。

items.body:
“The thing about playing the tuba in an orchestra is that you don’t have to play that much,” admitted composer Matthew Wright, who grew up playing the tuba in orchestras and funk bands, “but it’s the best seat in the house. You hear music back to front. The percussion and the brass are loud, so you hear all their detail, and the strings are this kind of ethereal thing that’s off in the distance.”

For the Kent-based Wright, who also improvises using turntables, samplers, and processers – most impactfully with Trance Map, his partnership with Evan Parker – this early realization nurtured a sensibility leading to the creation of immersive works that mix composition, improvisation, and technology. Cracked Glaze (False Walls) is a case in point, as it utilizes notated material – “dot music” is his good-humored term – improvisation, and Wright’s real-time sampling and processing immediately fed into surround sound, all of which he remixed for the CD.

Wright’s collaborators on Cracked Glaze represent various facets of his work. Ensemble Klang, an ensemble of mostly Dutch new music virtuosi, was an early champion of Wright’s compositions. Spheric Totemic is a Wright-instigated, flexibly configured improvising group with, on this occasion, Mandhira de Saram, Alexander Hawkins, Neil Charles and Stephen Davis. Sofia Jernberg, whose Musho with Hawkins was one of the brighter lights of 2024, is new to Wright’s constellation.

Historically, the conventional wisdom among exponents of freely improvised music is that the larger the group, the more apt the music will be muddied. It is a yardstick that is also prevalent among practitioners of contemporary composition. Individuality – of the improviser, of the composer – is more difficult to assert in or through a crowd. Although there are more than a dozen musicians heard on Cracked Glaze, there is no nebulous sprawl or complexity for complexity’s sake. Abstraction is tethered to figuration, the spine of the piece being a descending line that repeatedly submerges and reemerges, giving the interactions of voices clear relationships.

“In a lot of my written work for ensembles there is a central concern that tends to last a long period of time, an idea that will give the piece structure. I’m really interested in music being a kind of terrain that you can hear through and around, so that when you are listening, you are experiencing a kind of ‘visual’ situation. I guess this goes back to my work with vinyl records, because records make music a physical surface, where you can place the needle anywhere in the terrain of the music.

“In the improvised work, I don’t want to be the guy that says to improvisers, ‘this is how it goes.’ Improvisation, in a free context, is about distributed leadership. It’s about this beautiful situation of people saying, ‘the music could go here’ or ‘I hear the future of this music in what you’re playing,’ and the kind of listening that leads to those sorts of situations.

“Having the opportunity to work with a group that is mainly readers – Ensemble Klang – and a group that is mainly improvisers – Spheric Totemic – and Sofia Jernberg, gave me the opportunity to do something I haven’t done much of in my music, to have a spine that is unfurling but is always there. It doesn’t necessarily always have to be the main focus of the piece, but it will always be there. It will structure time in a certain way; improvisers can do whatever they want to do, and the music will be as much about them as it is the spine. I was really interested in having a sort of ‘object’ in the space of the improvisation. It’s almost like in the visual art world, where you have people moving around in a gallery but there’s a sculpture there. It’s in the room with you.”

Another virtue of Cracked Glaze is that it is the type of work that initially seems to come out of nowhere. It smacks of singularity. However, Wright’s backstory reveals that he did not come out of nowhere, as he has a pedigree linking him to England’s most consequential institutional incubator of experimental music, as well as its most venerable, living exponent of improvised music. Both associations largely account for how Wright’s disparate interests – several of which were common among Gen Xers in their formative years but were delayed in being assimilated into experimental music – were shaped into a mature aesthetic, and yielded in Cracked Glaze an arguably definitive statement.

“My experience, first of all, was writing music and playing in brass bands and funk bands and small improvising groups with friends,” Wright recently explained. “But I also liked writing chamber music for people who would take it away and play it somewhere else. I might not even be there for the performance. This background took me to study at the University of Huddersfield with the Professor who set up the Huddersfield Contemporary Music Festival, Richard Steinitz. I was very lucky. It was kind of random. He was my composition teacher. So, I was very lucky to have experiences like knocking on the door for a composition lesson and Richard Steinitz saying, ‘Ah, Matt, I can’t possibly teach you right now, but meet Karlheinz,’ and the door opens and there’s this world-famous composer from another generation that I had read about, but never dreamed I would meet.

“Contemporary classical music was a big part of my education, but I DJed as a kid. I was really interested at that point in the ‘80s and ‘90s when software, sampling, and DJ technology, was becoming affordable. It started showing up in people’s homes. Contemporary classical music and DJ culture were colliding in my mind when I was a kid. The only kind of formal education I could get was a classical education, along with some jazz theory, but it was largely based on dot music, written music. Then there was this other (non-written) side, like DJ culture and all of the great heritage of Black music that DJ culture is part of, and that was a kind of informal education I studied for myself.

“When I was a real little kid – like 12 or 13 – I made a lot of bedroom productions with a basic computer and turntable setup, really focused on instrumental hip-hop. I started to scratch around then, just watching how it was done on TV. My main inspirations were DJ Premier of Gangstarr, Terminator X of Public Enemy, and Maseo of De La Soul. When I was around 18 or 19, as a student, I DJed for a few parties, playing mainly funk, hip hop, and drum ‘n' bass. Around the same time – 1996-98 – I was in a few pop/funk bands that needed a DJ, so I did a few things with beat juggling and matching the pitch of the horns with turntable scratches, etc.

“In 1999 I DJed for a social event at the Huddersfield Contemporary Music Festival and I decided to just play fragments of music that I loved at the time: The Jazz Warriors, Louis Andriessen, Loose Tubes, Squarepusher, Björk. On the basis of that weird mix, I got the call to DJ at Abbey Road for the launch of a music charity, the PRS Foundation, in 2000. That was both a social event and included some (not entirely successful!) experimental scratching. When I moved to Holland to study with composer Louis Andriessen in 2002, I joined a trio with laptop artist Tom Tlalim and saxophonist Keir Neuringer – now of Irreversible Entanglements – and we played a few house parties and small gigs with our own mix of free improv and beat-based electronica. That same year the Huddersfield Festival commissioned ‘Presents from an Edited Then’ which was a 70-minute piece for The Apollo Saxophone Quartet and me DJing, designed for a club venue, again a mix of ‘social’ and ‘experimental’. That’s when I got interested in the worlds of contemporary classical music and DJ culture colliding.”

One of the first projects Wright embarked on was to compose for turntables and to teach classically-trained percussionists how to use them, integrating John Cage’s early work for percussion with the innovations of Christian Marclay and Otomo Yoshihide. “In a piece called Contact Theatre I had literally written out all of the material for notation-reading percussionists”, Wright said of the work. “If you look at a musical stave with the four spaces between the lines, I used those spaces to represent the four spaces on a vinyl record. The space that would be a F in the treble stave, that’s the space on the outer edge of the record, before any musical material appears on the vinyl record. All of the musical material on the record is included in the second space, and then the space at the center of the record was the third space, and then the label itself in the fourth space. You can prepare those spaces, put stickers on them. I would literally write percussion rhythms and they could produce those rhythms by dropping the needle on the record and get a ricochet effect or specify a section of the record I want to be played, say a saxophone solo three minutes into the record. I developed these ‘half-contact’ techniques where the needle sticks like a locked groove, and I taught the basics of hip hop scratching to percussionists, even though the music didn’t sound anything like hip hop.”

Wright then began to assess the proportions of and the relationships between the elements of his aesthetic and how to integrate them in his work. “Cracked Glaze is a collision of all of the above. I have been doing ensemble work and turntable work and installation work, but a lot of my focus is on the work with Evan in mixing and even post-production of the Trance Map material. Post-production is really part of the process, and Evan is very interested in exploring all that. Although Cracked Glaze doesn’t involve Evan, it brings to equal terms all of the sources I work with. There’s some notation written for Ensemble Klang with holes in that notation, space for the improvisation group of Spheric Totemic and Sofia Jernberg. They have start and stop times for the improvising, and they also sometimes have cues for some notation. I’m also mixing them live on stage, taking samples and remixing them and using the turntable as well. Then I take all that material and work on it a little in the studio, not to radically change the piece but to bring out some of the elements that you would hear live but not in a stereo recording. The piece brings together notation, improvisation, and technology, but not as separate forms. They all intersect. That’s where they all join on the map.”

In a roundabout way, the title of the piece speaks to the processes of its creation. It refers to the glazes used in high-fire ceramics that are formulated to crack on temperature; even though they are applied in an even manner, the cracking results in a surface that can be likened to a mosaic assembled with random tiles, with dark, hair-thin spaces between them. Though the results are subject to a unique firing, the experienced artist knows how to promote cracking that is pleasing and avoid cracking that ruins the piece.

“It may be interesting to talk about how jazz standards have worked in the past,” Wright responded to the idea of controlled cracking, and chuckling at the notion that he controlled the gas valve. “An excellent standard is one that can be played in its entirety and feel integrated and beautiful, but it is also a catalyst. It offers itself up to be cracked, to be turned into something new. In some ways, the use of notation to suggest a response is fascinating to me. On a technical level, there are definitely moments where I say to the improvisers, ‘at a certain point you will hear a line and at that point, that pitch, that’s your moment; if you’re improvising, the natural ebb and flow of the group will go to you’. But I don’t say ‘you should crack it’ to them; I say ‘it’s yours’.

“And there’s a third element there, the equivalent of the heat – the processing and the spatialization. I’m taking the feed of everybody, the notated music and the improvised music is coming to my setup, and I’m able to remix it and sample it. I’m an agent in the cracking, too. Whether it is notated or not is not the point, because it’s all going through the same system and being splintered into surround sound. That’s the third element, the sound design is a catalytic element.”

Wright pointed to a poster in his studio of a still influential Japanese textile exhibition he attended in his early 20s. “What I loved about that,” he said, “was that the dynamic shapes of these textiles are very rigid, spatially, but the textiles themselves have all sorts of holes in them. They are almost like fishing nets. I tried to create something similar by creating a structure that’s flexible but has holes in it. If we play this piece again, the melody line and the structure is going to be exactly the same every time and the improvising and the specialization will be different every time. That’s a long-winded way of saying I tried not to over notate.”

Wright acknowledged that post-production, particularly when the work was created in a surround sound environment and is remixed for stereo, creates a distinct experience of the work, and perhaps represents a new iteration of the pursuit of perfection in the studio, exemplified by Glenn Gould. “My pieces are concepts that have a sort of quantum existence,” Wright maintained. “What I mean is that if we are going to present the piece live, then there are circumstances that will be dynamic for the audience in the live space that may not be so dynamic when hearing it at home. In the live space, I’m dealing with surround sound. There are a whole lot of options to try to present that sort of experience in the stereo format. When it comes to making a CD or something online that people will listen to, I consider the domestic setting. I also consider that many people listen to music on the go, with headphones or their phone. You may be walking down the Avenue of the Americas and everything around you is changing, but there’s one consistent thread in the music.

“You have to consider the multiple ways that people listen now. I do hope that people will sit at home to listen to it. In that situation, it’s much closer to reading a book because it’s a solitary experience. You’re sitting with it for 40 or 50 minutes. Wearing headphones creates an interior experience. I really treasure those kinds of listeners and it’s a real privilege when someone spends that time with something that I’ve made with my musical friends.

“In the history of improvised music there have been many vehement statements about the relationship between free improvised music and recording. I totally get that, but I suppose that the question we now have to consider is what happens when you improvise with a recording. We don’t want the karaoke thing! How does the recording come back into the improvised music experience in as fluid a way you would have with another musician with an instrument? An instrument is obviously a technology of its own and the recording is the result of the technology. We need to make sure the technology is as flexible as any other instrument. The other thing I’m really fascinated by in the history of free creative music is the evolution of incorporating electronics. It’s really interesting for me when an electro-acoustic improvised situation might suggest that the music is not happening in the present tense, but in the past or the future.

“The thing I’m really interested in is those previously separated camps of notation, improvisation, and technology becoming one and the same, where there is an equaling out of the three. You’re not relying on one form of expression. And this seems to be causing a real revitalization of the scene, where people are mastering their separate disciplines and are also negotiating with each other. I think there’s more opportunity for creative music because of the dialogue between notation, improvisation, and technology. Looking for the connections between them is the main creative impetus. It’s not paper; it’s not technology; it’s not adherence to one way of making music. It’s about thinking about the connections between the people you’re working with. Saying ‘all of the above’ may be too easy an answer, but it does ascribe equal value to notation, improvisation and technology. These are all zones on the map and they all overlap each other, so the paths between those zones are what I’m interested in.”

***

Wright’s projects frequently overlap, the post production of one coinciding with the development of another. With summer approaching, Wright was mixing a duo session with Pat Thomas that has the flavor of This is Trickster; a Spheric Totemic album, and a Trance Map + recording on which Parker and him are joined by harpist Milana Zaric and Richard Barrett.

The presence of Barrett is particularly intriguing, as he pioneered improvised electronic music beginning in the 1990s – largely through FURT, his partnership with Paul Obermayer – laying groundwork for Wright and others. Additionally, Barrett’s compositions are renowned for testing – and often surpassing – the presumed physical limits of instrumentalists.

Barrett and Wright are part of a trajectory of composers foregrounding technology in their work. An earlier dot on the line, one that is essential but not obvious, is Conlon Nancarrow. The expatriate composer is the inspiration for Wright’s next major work, “Passing Nancarrow.” Wright’s latest project with the Belgian ensemble BL!NDMAN (the exclamation point is intentional) also has Hawkins in a key role. The piece debuts next year, marking 30 years since Nancarrow died.

“The idea of the piece is based around Nancarrow being obsessed with Art Tatum’s playing,” Wright explained. “He sampled Tatum in the form of piano rolls, using technology from a hundred years ago. What we will do is, while Alex improvises in real time, his notes are captured and this will trigger all sorts of reactions from the group. In a way, we turn Alex’s music into a piano roll.”

Wright was partly inspired by the writer and documentary film director Helen Borton’s comment that jazz and blues collide like a “hurricane” in Nancarrow’s music. Replace “hurricane” with “Nancarrow” and you get the gist of Wright’s conceptualization for the recording he is currently mixing – “four hurricanes of all kinds of crazy sounds.” Wright also considered the music of Squarepusher, Aphex Twin, and other exponents of electronic dance music, that influenced him when Nancarrow died in 1997, leading him to include “strange, intelligent dance music in the piece.”

However, the nexus of Nancarrow, Barrett, and Wright, is the consideration of the limits of music humans can create in real time, and how to get to the edge of those limits, if not extend them.

“Nancarrow reached for impossible, post-human music. But in my current work, I don’t have an artistic interest in post-human AI. I’ve heard a lot of AI-generated music and read a lot of AI research, and the thing I’m already bored by is that AI can do almost anything. Like a musician that can play everything and just won’t stop playing to give space for others, AI doing anything and everything is boring to me when you don’t hear inspired choices and you don’t hear the human labor or the human need for considered space in the music. But, I’m open minded. I just haven’t heard anything that inspires me yet. Back to the human level, in Alex’s piano playing, there is that reaching beyond what is supposedly humanly possible, to reach a new vista for what is possible.

“You can say that, for his times, Nancarrow was making a post-human kind of music, but we should remember that he sat there, punching holes. So, I don’t hear a sort of pre-AI in his music, a piano that can do anything, but the blood and the hours of Nancarrow sitting maybe six months to create an explosive two minutes. I want to know how humans feel when they hear music and when they make music. If that is aided by technology, the idea is that the technology helps musical thinking like an instrument helps musical thinking. My interest in technology is the same as Alex’s interest in the piano, there’s a tradition of human tool use there that in a sense heightens the human listening experience if done successfully.

“Another thing I like about Nancarrow was that he was true to his beliefs, which is why he left the US for Mexico City, which resulted in him working in relative isolation. He just got on with it. A few people had experimented with the player piano before, but he made it his own. I appreciate that you can hear the edges in music and you’re OK with not being able to know everything beyond that edge. I guess the difference between the scene we have now and Nancarrow’s situation is that we can go to the edge together in a collaborative spirit.”

items._cn_summary: Matthew Wright 的《Cracked Glaze》融合记谱作曲、自由即兴与实时采样处理，经环绕声混音后呈现于 CD。专辑联合荷兰新音乐团体 Ensemble Klang、自由即兴组合 Spheric Totemic 以及歌手 Sofia Jernberg 等十余人参与录制。面对大编制带来的浑浊风险，Wright 以一条持续下沉又反复重现的旋律主线作为骨架，将抽象与形象化材料紧密关联，使众多声部之间形成清晰的呼应关系。他将即兴视为分布式领导，强调乐手间的相互聆听与音乐走向的共同塑造；同时借由黑胶唱片的物质隐喻，把音乐构想为可穿行其间的听觉地形。整体听感兼具沉浸感与结构感，是当代实验即兴与电子手段结合的一次扎实实践。

items.body: Listening to “adventurous” music can be a hazardous activity. It often prompts a familiar question from unsuspecting visitors: “What is this noise?” toppe bianche 白色补丁 by Li Song / Luciano Maggiore begins precisely at that point of uncertainty, asking not only how one should listen to a work, but whether listening can ever be separated from the circumstances in which it takes place. Recorded beneath the railway arches and across the marshes of Walthamstow, London, the album functions as a negotiation between portable electronics, passing trains, weather, wildlife, and human activity. Consisting of two long-form mirror pieces, “/ * /” and “* / *“, the album is built around simple materials: glissandi, friction-like textures, environmental sounds, and interludes of white noise. The title, which translates as “White Patches”, refers to the masking processes used in post-production and the way the different sounds are connected. Trains become white noise, while birdsong, distant conversations, footsteps and accidental events drift in and out of focus. As the artists themselves insist, there is no background here. Everything is present all the time. What soon becomes apparent is the way toppe bianche 白色补丁 refuses to privilege any single element. The portable speakers generating the glissandi are no more important than the arch itself, the trains overhead, or the occasional passer-by. The music exists in a state between composition and improvisation, intention and accident. The sounds feel fragile, yet stubbornly present. They neither demand attention nor disappear entirely. For those not having a tape deck, headphones might reveal the intricate layering of the recording. Personally, I feel the album especially rewarding when played through my laptop speakers in an ordinary domestic environment especially on hot summer days. With windows open, street noise, birds outside, distant traffic, even the hum of household appliances become inadvertent extensions of the piece. In this sense, Toppe Bianche is not simply a recording but a framework for listening. Like the cliché of the tree falling in the forest, it raises questions about perception and presence. The glissandi may occasionally vanish beneath trains, white noise or the sounds of one’s own surroundings, but they continue to exist. That quiet insistence may be the album’s most radical gesture. In the following interview conducted by email Li Song and Luciano Maggiore elaborate on the production process. Li Song and Luciano Maggiore This recording was made beneath the railway arches and across the marshes of Walthamstow, with passing trains becoming an integral part of the sound world. Rather than attempting to isolate yourselves from the environment, you chose to add white noise and work with it. How did the location shape the music, and at what point did the surrounding sounds cease to be “background” and become collaborators in the piece? Luciano Maggiore: The simple fact that we chose to use that arch in the marshes says a lot about how much we wanted the recording to be entangled with the place. It’s a place we both know quite well, having been the location of a small, almost spontaneous festival of experimental music organised by a few friends and us some years ago. The main characters in the work are, of course, the sounds produced by us during the acts of recording and post-production, but the flesh of the pieces, and the world they inhabit, is that arch itself, with its inhabitants and all the accidents imposed by the surrounding sonic life. There is no background. Everything is present all the time. Li Song: Both Luciano and I are quite familiar with the space itself. A couple of years back, the two of us and some friends did an outdoor show under the exact same arch. We both live near the marshes but in opposite directions, so I wouldn’t be surprised if the arch is actually the midpoint between our homes in London. When we decided to record outdoors, that was the first space that came to mind. I think the location sort of designed the piece, in a way we didn’t expect it to at the start. We had chatted about the idea of masking very early on, which is putting one audio signal on top of another to cover it up. But then we sort of forgot about it and went down the route of recording glissandos under the arch. Later on, while working with the recordings, the idea came back to us. The white noise masking, around and over with the train, holds the pieces together. The album is described as existing between composition and improvisation, and between human dialogue and environmental processes. Can you talk about how decisions were made during the recording? Were there agreed structures, or did the piece emerge through listening and reacting to each other, the trains, and the acoustics of the space? LM: The pieces had a backbone that was decided a priori: the use of glissandos, a series of movements through the space, and a range of frequencies we could work with in both pieces. Decisions were then made in situ, following recording attempts and small trials and errors, to understand whether the choices made beforehand suited the situation we found ourselves in. I would say the core idea was to use digital glissandos and, later, fields of white noise to mask certain parts of the recordings. Li Song built a simple piece of software that was easy to control, with an array of parameters (frequency and duration, if I remember correctly). We performed with the software using our phones, each connected to an identical Bluetooth speaker. LS: If I remember correctly, we only had the moving glissando idea and the location planned out. We left pretty much everything else to the day of the recording. Both of us are quite flexible and just open to seeing what happens. I had programmed an oscillator app on a webpage so we could use our portable speakers to generate the glissando sounds. That’s the continuous sound you hear in the recordings, where you can change the pitch range and certain timing settings. On the day, I showed Luciano how to use it, and we briefly talked about how we would move around the space. We did maybe two or three sessions with different settings and configurations. I feel like as we recorded the latter half, we started improvising more and ignoring the rules we had set at the beginning. After that, we just went home to listen back and work on it later. It was during that later process that we had the masking idea with white noise to go along with the train sounds. It didn’t take us long to find an alternative way to mask the other track, and I think the two tracks work better together. Li, your work with No Performance often seeks to minimise the presence of the performer, while Luciano’s practice frequently examines performance itself, repetition, endurance and the theatricality of sound production. How did these seemingly different approaches interact during this collaboration? Did either of you find yourselves working outside your usual habits? LM: Even though our approaches may appear different, both of us perform in various formations that use performativity as a way of staging situations involving sound. Li Song often performs with the artist Mengting Zhuo, and both of us are part of a trio with On Yee Lo, among other collaborations. I would say that neither of us felt in any way out of place LS: The ‘No Performance’ idea actually started out as a series of experiments that Zhu Wenbo and I were doing in Beijing back in 2015. We were doing pieces where the computer listened to acoustic instruments and did its own thing according to the program we had designed beforehand. It was maybe a half-joke to name it ‘No Performance’ because I would just start the program and sit there doing nothing. To be honest, we eventually explored other ideas beyond this style. So it’s not some strict rule I follow throughout all my music. Having said that, I do feel I have grown more attached to the idea of letting things perform by ‘themselves.’ I do believe that somehow shows in this music too. Maybe you could say the different approaches work in different dimensions. I think our approaches overlap more than what it looks like. The liner notes mention a desire to create a music that “eschews self-awareness in favour of a supernatural imbalance.” That is a striking phrase. What does “supernatural imbalance” mean to you in this context? Is it connected to unpredictability, to the agency of the environment, or to a more philosophical idea of dissolving control? LM: That’s a beautiful way of describing the work, but we can’t really claim ownership of the phrase. I think I understand what Cai and Yizhuo (the owners of Aloe) are implying with it, but I would rather leave any explanation to them. LS: To me, my first impression when hearing the track after we add the studio material was actually a sense of balance. Just like the album title, the patch holds things together. Listening to the album, there are moments where it becomes difficult to distinguish between performer, device, environmental sound and recording artefact. Both of your practices seem interested in questioning authorship and intentionality. Do you see this blurring of boundaries as a political gesture, an aesthetic one, or simply the most honest way of engaging with sound today? LM: I’m not sure about honesty. I don’t personally think of what I do as particularly political. There are, of course, other, more effective ways of making a statement than using music to do so. I’m conscious that every position I take in this world carries political value and therefore implies a certain stance. However, I am concerned with music making and the ways in which it can be staged. I believe in making music for music’s sake. LS: I think this is just naturally how we work. With computer or electronic music, there’s a huge appreciation for high-fidelity audio and how many channels you have in your system. For me, ever since my time in Beijing, I’ve performed with my laptop in people’s living rooms, playing through a bunch of cheap small speakers I found for 30 RMB each on Taobao. Not everyone has access to a 16-channel speaker system, and more importantly, there’s just music for laptop speakers. Luciano and I also worked together on the ‘unspecified unspecified unspecified’ concert series in London for a year after COVID. We had this rule of self-amplification, where performers were solely responsible for amplifying their own sound if they needed to. I suppose that’s also related to this idea: people working with their own things, in the space they are given. What is the significance of the title toppe bianche 白色补丁? LM: The Italian toppe bianche can be roughly translated into English as “white patches”. I believe that 白色补丁 is read and understood in more or less the same way. LS: I already referred to title holding things in the above answers, it matches what we were doing with the studio material in the end. (Gianmarco Del Re)
items._genre: experimental / field recording / sound art / electroacoustic
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑在伦敦沃尔瑟姆斯托的铁路拱门下与沼泽地中录制，由便携电子设备、过境火车、天气、野生动物与人类活动共同构成完整声音世界。两位艺术家以滑音、摩擦质感与环境声为基础材料，搭配白噪声过渡段，拒绝将任何单一元素置于主导地位，使作品游走于作曲与即兴、意图与意外之间。标题"白色补丁"指向后期制作中的遮蔽处理方式——火车化为白噪声，鸟鸣、远距离对话、脚步声与偶然事件在焦点内外漂移。对这张作品而言，没有真正的背景，一切同时在场。专辑的激进之处在于提出一个问题：当滑音被火车或周围环境吞没时，它仍然存在。录音不只是声音文件，而是一种聆听框架，邀请听众将自身的日常环境纳入作品之中。

items.body:
Key Chicago house architect Ron Trent departs the club for the bedroom under new alias La Marr, a new vent for his most romantic, sublime soundscapes, warmly advised FFO Detroit Escalator Company, Terre Thaemlitz, Wally Badarou, Klaus Schulze, MvO Trio

Light candles/incense and scatter petals for optimal effect when immersing in La Marr’s debut ‘Mood Programs’ EP, which finds a perfect home nestled amid Music From Memory’s precious, timeline-twining cuts of new age ambient, kosmiche, and Balearic wist. It’s also a natural, logical progression from the sort of depths usually secreted in Trent’s albums, but here given full sides to unfurl their functions, which we’re sure will also sound dead tasty, syrupy slow, on 33-not-45. 

He paints the lushest 12 min panorama of elliptical stereo pads, floating organ cloud structures and skin-stroke arps in ‘Good Magic’, edging on similar terrain to Terre Thaemlitz’s golden revision of Tangerine Dream’s ‘Love on a Real Train’, where a fine line of hand played drums emphasises the swaying groove - swooning either bed-ways or a little rug-cut, depending on your disposition - before ‘Clear’ hustles a palette of the slinkiest Afro-Latinate, Brazilian rhythms under big, dusky skies, hinting at Manuel Göttsching via MvO Trio. 

Your ears do not deceive you: this one is proper lush.
items._genre: ambient / deep house / new age / kosmische / balearic
items._cn_summary: 芝加哥浩室建筑师Ron Trent以新别名La Marr推出首张EP《Mood Programs》，将俱乐部语境延伸至卧室与冥想空间。专辑由Music From Memory发行，属于新纪元氛围、Kosmische与巴利亚里怀旧氛围的范畴，强调以33转慢速播放时的沉浸体验。首曲《Good Magic》以十二分钟构建椭圆立体声pad、悬浮管风琴云层与手鼓律动，呈现极简而宽广的声场；《Clear》引入非洲-拉丁与巴西节奏元素，铺展于朦胧音景之下。整体制作偏柔缓、浪漫、氛围化，是一次从浩室根基向慢速冥想电子的延伸实验，适合长时间低音量聆听。

items.body:
Finally, Kompakt issue a true GAS outlier on vinyl for the first time, recorded in 1989 and containing some of Wolfgang Voigt’s earliest and starkest recycling of magisterial Wagner loops, closest to the ends of The Caretaker, Philip Jeck, Kevin Drumm.

One of those releases that has lurked on our shelves since 2008 as a book and CD, ‘November 89’ exists in the margins of Wolfgang Voigt’s GAS canon as its creepiest and most occluded evocation of long walks in the Bavarian forests. While other GAS classics ooze a sort of dappled warmth breaking thru the trees in their widescreen dub techno strolls, you can fully feel the light dying over the horizon and the forest drawing in on this particularly gloomy, hour-long suite. 

As the title suggests, it was mostly, remarkably, made in ’89, back when Voigt was finding his feet between techno, house and indie-pop, and nearly a decade before he co-founded Kompakt with Michael Mayer & Jürgen Paape - by which time he was a full-fledged rave dynamo as Love Inc. and myriad others notable projects. And, in that sense, it can be heard as his ‘Selected Ambient Works 89-95’ - or perhaps more pertinently with SAW II vibes - in his nascent attempt to chase the ambient dragon, which surely endures for its strangely nostalgic, unheimlich qualities.

An educated guess leads us to think the first three were made in ’89, taking in the nightfall scenery of smudged symphonic strings and icy crackle to ‘Der Wald’, plus the muddied bass waltz and spectral pall of ‘Das Moor’, thru the self-evidently titled centrepiece ‘1989-11-01’, bristling with a digitally iridescent dread. ‘Tal 90’ and ‘Nah Und Fern’, which shares its title with the 2008 boxset, were most likely made a little later, and find the wintry doom thawing to the GAS-eous forms we’ve all come to deeply know and adore. 

A true evergreen for deep ambient techno connoisseurs, no less
items._genre: ambient / dark ambient / experimental electronic / drone
items._cn_summary: GAS的《November 89》是Wolfgang Voigt早期作品的首次黑胶发行，录制于1989年，介于techno、house与独立流行之间的探索阶段。这张专辑呈现出与GAS后期作品不同的面貌——没有温暖阳光穿透树林的宽银幕dub techno漫步，而是巴伐利亚森林中光线消逝、暮色合拢的阴沉意象。专辑以瓦格纳式循环采样为核心素材，融合模糊的交响弦乐、冰冷噼啪噪音与泥泞的低音漩涡，营造出一种怀旧而不安的异化氛围。前三首据信作于1989年，呈现夜幕降临的风景，后两首稍晚创作，融入了后来GAS标志性的温暖形式。整张专辑时长约一小时，是deep ambient techno领域的常青之作，展现了Voigt在创立Kompakt厂牌之前对ambient语言的早期实验。

items.excerpt: Field Records’ treasured Monolake reissue program yields a first vinyl cut of the influential project’s 2nd album - the last as a duo of Robert Henke & Gerhard Behles, before the latter turned attention wholly to developing Ableton Live software. Genuine landmark stuff for electronica fiends In suit with the reissued ‘Hong Kong’ (1997) comp of early EPs for Chain Reaction, and the self-released debut LP ‘Gravity’ (2001), comes ‘Interstate’; one of Monolake’s most distinctive entries in the space
items.body:
Field Records’ treasured Monolake reissue program yields a first vinyl cut of the influential project’s 2nd album - the last as a duo of Robert Henke & Gerhard Behles, before the latter turned attention wholly to developing Ableton Live software. Genuine landmark stuff for electronica fiends

In suit with the reissued ‘Hong Kong’ (1997) comp of early EPs for Chain Reaction, and the self-released debut LP ‘Gravity’ (2001), comes ‘Interstate’; one of Monolake’s most distinctive entries in the space where dub techno met concrète sound design and hypermodern electronica. The 65 minute album sees Henke & Behles ultimately conclude a vision of a semi-organic techno architecture that transcends club, home, and can listening, thanks to their judicious balance of whirring, syncopated grooves and custom-built, elemental sound design that feels remarkably future-proofed, then and now, 

In historic terms the duo follow a line of activated electronic systems from David Tudor to Lee “Scratch” Perry, Vince Clarke to Uwe Schmidt, Basic Channel and Autechre, by breathing vivid, imaginary life and space into circuitry and code. More specifically, in Monolake’s hands, everything teems with insectoid detail and a fascinating depth perception, conjuring immersive environments one can take as much pleasure from dancing to as simply admiring its elegantly awesome architexture. 

The relatively new freedoms of Max/MSP software and the pair’s ever heightened proprioception allowed them to enact forms of impossible physics that dance into hyperspace between the air-stepping lushness of ‘abundance’ and needlepoint D&B abstractions ‘ginza’ or ‘terminal’, showcasing sheer, advanced tekkerz on ‘gecko’ and serving the ‘floor with nexx-level depths on two parts of ‘tangent’, plus the metallic electro ping-pong of ‘perpetuum’ and 10 mins of proto-virtual reality in ‘amazon.’
items._genre: dub techno / experimental electronic / sound design / IDM
items._cn_summary: Monolake第二张专辑首次以黑胶形式再版，呈现了Robert Henke与Gerhard Behles在二人组时期对半有机化电子声响架构的探索。专辑将dub techno与具体音乐式的声学设计相融合，65分钟的篇幅中既有轻盈繁复的碎拍抽象，也有针尖般精密的鼓打贝斯解构，以及近十分钟的前虚拟现实音景。借助Max/MSP软件赋予的创作自由，两位音乐家将电路与代码转化为充满昆虫般微观细节与深邃空间感的声音环境，构建出既适合舞池也适合专注聆听的跨界作品。从David Tudor到Basic Channel的电子音乐谱系在此被延续并向前推进，是电子音乐领域兼具历史意义与前瞻性的里程碑之作。

items.body:
Future modal jazz dub, heard thru a Y2K lens by legendary blowers Pharaoh Sanders & Graham Haynes, and diffused in Bill Laswell’s illbient dub style & pattern. A slept-on, cross-generational ace sure to pique interest FFO Jon Hassell to Talvin Singh, Lászlo Hortobágyi to Material.

Cooked up in NYC’s jazz crucible in 2003 as a duo of Sanders & Haynes - now re-mantled as a Sanders x Laswell session for its first vinyl cut - ‘With a Heartbeat’ speaks to the rich confluence of deeply rooted, forward-thinking jazz with ambient dub that tilted from the late C.20th into this century. Centred on the human heartbeat, it unfurls at a rested systolic throb in two landscaped-scale works which bookend deeper dives into Indian raga and tabla actions, the latter of which may find favour on open-minded ‘floors, due to its effortless, toes-off-the-ground levity. But essentially, it’s idealised for floating at home or road tripping on the astral highway.

Bill Laswell’s name at the top signifies his integral input, but with no discount to Graham Hayne’s cornet, beautifully knit in warm, rising air with his peer, pioneering tenor sax player Pharaoh Sanders, who brings a half century of chops with Coltrane, Sharrock, and myriad others, to the plate. Quite simply it’s a lush listen from front to back, opening from heartical subbass pulse into 17 mins of dusted illbient dub with a cool reserve on ‘Across Time’, and shoring up in almost big beat 4th world fusion scapes reminding of the eL-Hortobãgyi Hortator album with ‘Gamaka’.

Yet we’re most partial to the midsection, where Sanders & Haynes colour the luxuriant space and rolling ballast with a wider range of brass and woodwind in the dewy raga of ‘Morning Tala’, and Trilok Gurtu’s undulating and spicy tabla and scatting vox evoke an aerial game of hashed-out kabaddi in ‘Alankara’.
items._genre: free jazz / illbient dub / world fusion / ambient
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是爵士与电子融合的跨界之作，核心围绕心跳脉搏展开，节奏松弛而绵长。Pharoah Sanders的次中音萨克斯与Graham Haynes的短号在Bill Laswell的illbient混音手法中交织，形成温暖升腾的音色对话。作品分为两大长篇结构，中间穿插印度拉格与塔布拉鼓元素，Trilok Gurtu的塔布拉演奏与即兴人声在'Alankara'中营造出空中搏击般的律动。整张专辑融合了自由爵士的即兴传统、dub的低频质感与世界音乐的色彩，适合在冥想、旅途中聆听。从音乐理念来看，它延续了Coltrane以来爵士与东方音乐对话的脉络，同时以电子手法拓展了声音空间，体现了2000年代纽约地下场景对爵士边界的探索。

items.body:
‘hej!’ is the hauntingly hyperreal first album proper by Felicita, for PC Music.

Arriving 5 years since Felicita’s beguiling ‘(>’.’)>#’ and ‘Frenemies’ releases took us by surprise with their lacquered textures and uncannily poignant arrangements, ‘hej!’ claims their place in the same dimensions as Arca, Sophie and 0PN with a highly personalised expression of hyperreal modernity.

Polish folk, trance, trap and and classical chamber music are melded into the same mutant body of music with deceptively effortless appeal that’s both pop-wise and avant, charming and at times unsettling thru its juxtapositions of new and old. 

Warbling keys haunt much of the album, but in a way that swerves the poshness of, say Nils Frahm and co, for a more surreal and unreal effect, especially when he adds in snatches of processed Polish folk song, and then sharply switches to needling electronics, as with the vacuum sealed hyper reggaeton of ‘coughing up amber’, while the melodic couplet of ‘soft power I + II’ feel paradoxically timeless yet right in the pregnant here-and-now, though their pastoral field recordings came from a computer game, rather than the real thing.

The salty blatz of ’shook’ is a tart palate cleanser at the centre of the album, bristling with an outright aggression that contrast the rest of the set, particularly the eerie highlight of Caroline Polachek’s take on ‘marzipan’, an old Polish folk song reinterpreted with lustrous Reese-like bass and synthetic strings, while the sickening rush of ‘night soil (fade out)’ recalls the devil in the detail noise of Croww, and the closing ‘Mosaic’ elicits a most curious synthesis of emotions - ecstasy, fear, and romance in it’s fleeting choral cadence.
items._genre: hyperpop / experimental electronic / avant-pop / folk-trance fusion
items._cn_summary: 这是Felicita在PC Music厂牌发行的首张正式专辑，将波兰民间音乐、trance、trap与古典室内乐熔铸成高度失真的后现代声响体。制作中频繁使用处理过的波兰民歌片段与尖锐电子切换，形成新与旧的并置张力。键盘音色游走于荒诞与超现实之间，刻意回避Nils Frahm式的学院派优雅。Caroline Polachek重新诠释的波兰民歌'marzipan'以合成弦乐与Reese低音重构民谣根基，'night soil (fade out)'借鉴微观噪音质感，'Mosaic'以短暂合唱段落综合狂喜、恐惧与浪漫。整体呈现五年磨一剑的成熟度，将地方传统与全球实验美学无缝焊接。

items.body:
Wah Wah Wino​'s Davy Kehoe, Morgan Buckley and Olmo are joined by avant legend Roger Doyle, among others, on a delectably brilliant, 54 minute collage, re-upped with new artwork for 2026.

An ode to the putative pleasures of ketamine, ‘KWALK’ emulates the effect of everyone’s fave equine dissociative with a mazy disarray of folk rock, ambient electronics and balmy, bandy-legged grooves bent for getting ketty with it. Inside, song structures quiesce to smeared samples and fractal lines of thought perhaps familiar to anyone who’s done a bump or two.

As with all WIno joints, normal logic is out the window, replaced by a loosey goosey slant that's a real pleasure to follow. In their slippery snakes ’n ladders chicanery, ‘KWALK’ recalls everything from Davy Kehoe's endlessly-rinsed 'Storm Desmond' to the Lost Highway OST, The KLF’s 'Chill Out' to Sigtryggur Berg Sigmarsson & BJ NIlsen’s ‘Avantgardegasse’ ace thru to Don Cherry’s communal free jazz jams and Laura Cannell’s folk flights in our minds, and should be considered a go-to slab for those times when the sofa’s on the ceiling and everyone’s too munted to pick another tune.

We have a special place in our hearts for mixtapes/collage pieces pressed to vinyl - and this one is prob the best we've heard since John T. Gast's 'Invocations II' set for Blowing Up The Workshop a few years back.
items._genre: experimental collage / ambient electronics / folk rock / free jazz
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑以54分钟的拼贴作品形式展开，试图模拟氯胺酮带来的迷幻与脱节感。制作团队将民谣摇滚、氛围电子、模糊采样与自由爵士片段并置，歌曲结构被有意消解，取而代之的是松散流动的声音迷宫。评论将其与The KLF的《Chill Out》、Lost Highway原声、Don Cherry的集体即兴以及John T. Gast的作品并置，强调其在实体唱片中实现拼贴美学的稀有价值。整体逻辑被悬置，声音在不同体裁间滑移，既包含Davy Kehoe标志性的循环旋律，也融入avant传奇Roger Doyle的前卫声响。对于偏好实验拼贴、氛围即兴与跨类型融合的听众而言，这是一张在沙发颠倒时仍能持续运转的唱片。

items.body:
The momentous Chain Reaction full-length debut by Robert Henke and Gerhard Behles aka Monolake, issued on vinyl for the very first time on its 25th anniversary and still sounding as sleekly futuristic as ever.

Replete in its definitive remastered edition, which features additional field recordings of rain and insects on ‘Cyan’, Monolake’s debut album is a masterclass of late ‘90s techno straddling widescreen ambient soundscapes and pulsing, Berlin-standard dub techno. It gathers tracks from 1996’s preceding 12” releases, ‘Cyan’, ‘Lantau /Macao’, and ‘Occam / Arte’ plus ‘Index’ from his Helical Scan project, in a landmark album that, with hindsight, can be heard as a milestone between early ‘90s ambient techno and subsequent, sleeker forms of minimalism and spatialized sound design that reflected and deeply influenced techno and electronic music to come.

The re-edit of ‘Cyan’, teeming with insectoid nanorhythms and the patter of rain, opens a seminal set that distills the head-long energy of ‘90s techno to a blissful sublime without losing its vital propulsion. In the tunnelling dynamic of ‘Index’ thru the exquisitely light-footed stepper ‘Occam’ he conceives a sort of techno purism comparable with Basic Channel but distinguished by its relatively crisp contours and HD definition. But he also proves equally adept at other routes and branches of techno, as with the slow, heaving designs of ‘Lantau / Macau’, which impressionistically convey his times spent in the Far East through mutated field recordings, while the radiant ‘Arte’ is a masterpiece of downtempo ambient techno, and ‘Mass Transit Railway’ ropes in fellow synth fiend Wieland Samolak, who wrote user manuals and their translations for Emu Systems and Sequential Circuits - for a floating high-water mark of ‘90s ambient ambient sound design.
items._genre: ambient techno / dub techno / minimalism / sound design / field recording
items._cn_summary: Monolake首张专辑《Hongkong》25周年纪念黑胶再版，收录了1996年前后发行的多张12寸单曲中的曲目，经重新母带处理后更加清晰立体。专辑以宽阔的氛围音景为基底，融合柏林标准的dub techno律动，穿插田野录音——尤其是《Cyan》中重新编辑的雨声与昆虫纳米节奏，开篇即营造出沉浸式听觉体验。《Index》展现隧道式的动态推进，《Occam》则以轻盈的舞步体现了techno纯粹主义。《Lantau/Macau》通过变形的田野录音印象派式地呈现远东经历，《Arte》是downtempo氛围techno的杰作，《Mass Transit Railway》与合成器专家合作，达成90年代氛围声音设计的浮动高点。整张专辑被视为90年代ambient techno与后续极简主义及空间化声音设计之间的里程碑。

items.body:
Dreader than dread dub vapors from Ghost Dubs, in a lineage stretching from Dadawah to Burial Mix, Vainqueur to Resilent, Pole to Rod Modelll...​

Toiling in Berlin’s deep seam of abstract dub practice that scrolls back to Rhythm & Sound’s earliest via Pole’s dusty convections and Chain Reaction's fritzed mutations; Ghost Dubs embodies the art of dub as method with a strong haul of dematerialised, sludgy tramplers operating close to the scuzzy heart of Kevin Martin, aka The Bug. Uncompromisingly in-the-zone and dank as a bong, the dozen cuts get right under the skin, up-the-pharynx, with an intoxicatingly sedated and hallucinatory quality that impresses murky, vaporous patterns on the back of blunted eyelids and may possibly raise knees to its slompy skank and imaginary physics. 

Of course, the sound is rooted in the innovative, half century-old traditions of Jamaican dub, as established by King Tubby and Lee “Scratch” Perry, and developed by the likes of Scientist or Mad Professor. But Ghost Dubs picks it up at the point where it diffused into techno and noise during the ‘90s, taking that sound as a jump-off into his microcosm of granular, atomised atmospheric disintegration that nevertheless holds to a steady ballast of scoop-worrying sub-bass tremors. No doubt anyone who’s followed the devolution of this sound outside Jamaica, from NYC illbient to Berlin dub techno, will recognise his hands-on-desk tekkerz ushering the sound into oblique new spaces with a canny sense of proprioception that locates it somewhere in fissure between classic and contemporary soundspheres.

From the caustic attrition of ‘Chemical’, thru the inverted mulch of ‘Dub Lobotomy’, to the sensuous but elephantine trample of ‘Hot Wired’ and tumescent swell of ‘Circles Lines’ ,Ghost Dubs leaves his clammy fingerprint on every cut. Some are primed to bend your Clarks, as with the bilgy step of ‘The Regulator’, and airborne skank of ‘Thin Line’, and the harness-tugging pressure of ‘Dub Battle’, but they’re all held in check with a overarching slowness that gels the 12 tracks as a proper end-to-end listen in the manner of Pole’s early albums with a deeply reliable robustness and temper that stakes it out as arguably canonic tackle.

items.body: Review by WaldoJeffers — As someone who really enjoys Conrad Schnitzler's early work with Kluster, Tangerine Dream and also solo, I consider "Gold" to be a highly convincing album, standing in the tradition of "Blau" and certainly "Rot", dating from the same creative period as this belatedly released album.Schnitzler experiments here once again with all sorts of electronically generated instruments; briefly, I even hear an accordion. You will search in vain for rhythms and harmonies here, of course; "Gold" is an album of free form. It chirps, pings and creaks merrily away; only in track 12 (the tracks have no titles) does something almost akin to a dance mood arise as a result of the electronic percussion; although even to this you can hardly dance, there is simply too much going on. An oriental-sounding flute improvises over heavy chirping and bubbling above the quasi-soloing percussion. Space techno? With the following track, "13", which sounds like a cool, empty factory hall turned into music, a bit of Industrial also comes into play."Gold" is fun and enormously entertaining for those people who (like me) find many of the productions of the "Berlin School" incredibly boring. Not a typical Conrad Schnitzler album, but for me (perhaps for that very reason) one of the best.
items._genre: experimental electronic / Berlin school / industrial / free improvisation
items._cn_summary: 康拉德·施尼茨勒这张《Gold》延续了他与Kluster、 Tangerine Dream合作时期的实验脉络，与《Blau》《Rot》属于同一创作阶段。整张专辑完全脱离传统节奏与和声框架，属于自由形态的电子即兴创作，合成器音色不停发出啁啾、叮咚与吱嘎声，间或出现手风琴、东方风格的笛子等非常规电子拟音。第十三轨以空旷厂房般的回响引入工业元素；第十二轨则是全专辑最接近舞曲氛围的一首，电子打击乐叠加重音与气泡般的合成器声部，呈现出太空科技舞曲的雏形。专辑不追求结构完整，而是以大量密集的声响事件推动聆听体验。对于厌烦柏林学派程式化制作模式的听众而言，这张专辑提供了更具娱乐性与实验性的替代选择。

items.body: Review by A Crimson Mellotron — ProjeKct Three's 'Masque' comes straight from the R&D department of King Crimson. This is the thirdinstallment in the live project series featuring members of the 'THRAK' lineup of the Robert Fripp-led band, brought together with the aim of exploring off-beat ideas through improvisation andexperimentation. These are live recordings featuring alternating lineups of the 90s Crimson, withthis particular 1999 recording featuring the trio of Robert Fripp, Trey Gunn, and Pat Mastelotto. Asis the case with the majority of the KC releases from that period, the music played by ProjeKctThree incorporates the spacey ambient soundscapes patented by Fripp, together with the finely tunedWarr guitar of Trey Gunn and the impressive array of electronic percussion and loops played by PatMastelotto. The type of experimental rock presented on 'Masque', however, is more abstract and lessgroovy than the output of other ProjeKcts (like One or Two, which makes it closer to something like'Thrakattak' than the album 'THRAK' itself.The thirteen tracks making up this live album are numbered and (perhaps suggestively) left untitled,while the somewhat intimidating, surreal and impersonal cover art uncannily reflects the kind ofmusic played on 'Masque'. This is one of these experimental recordings that only make sense whenheard in their entirety, but if I were to outline several pieces of greater significance, I wouldhave to start with '1', which is an obnoxious and impulsive opener, replete with hefty bass tonesand obscure guitar licks. 'Masque 2' then presents a more sustained rock sound tinted with gentleambient soundscapes, while the complex rhythms on '3' weave around the haunting electronics in arather menacing way. Later on, 'Masque 7' represents another abstract-sided piece, impressing with asoft but prominent bass sound, whereas the industrial hue encompassing 'Masque 8' makes it one ofthe darker compositions heard on this album. It is also worth noting how effective the hypnoticallyabrasive sounds on '9' are, with the two final pieces also being among the highlights.Of all the ProjeKcts, Three might be the single most intriguing variation of Crimson - 'Masque' isunorthodox and compelling, but for me this is the kind of experimentation that drives the genreforward.
items._cn_summary: ProjeKct Three是King Crimson在90年代末推出的实验子项目，《Masque》是其1999年的现场录音，由Fripp、Gunn和Mastelotto三人组合完成。与其他ProjeKct相比，这张作品的抽象程度更高，Groove感更弱，更接近《Thrakattak》而非《THRAK》本身。整张专辑由十三首编号曲目组成，呈现了Fripp标志性的太空感氛围音景、Gunn的Warr吉他以及Mastelotto的电子打击乐与循环声效。乐评特别提到了开篇曲目的粗粝低频与模糊吉他线条、第二首的持续性摇滚框架与柔和氛围、第七首的抽象低音质感、第八首的工业色调以及第九首的催眠式摩擦声响。评论者认为这张作品是所有ProjeKct中最具吸引力的一次变体，实验性强且具有推动整个流派前进的意义。

items.body: It took the Norwegian duo Kant Kino nearly nine years to release their fourth album. Despite this lengthy hiatus, EBM fans are unlikely to have forgotten the band, as their previous full-length releases were polished, expertly crafted examples of the genre. While EBM remains the album’s primary influence, “Echoes Of The End” also ventures into other sonic territories. The result is a compelling fusion of EBM and Electro-Pop, with occasional touches of Future-Pop. Some tracks recall the melodic approach of Assemblage 23, while the album’s darker moments evoke the early work of Skinny Puppy. At its core, however, “Echoes Of The End” remains a hard-hitting, relentless EBM record, impeccably executed and enriched with vintage-inspired synth textures. The powerful yet controlled vocal delivery perfectly complements the album’s atmosphere. We are treated to no fewer than 24 tracks, although for me the collection is ultimately defined by the irresistible “Choice.” Kant Kino is back—and not a moment too soon. While their sound has evolved, they continue to deliver EBM of the highest caliber. (Rating:8½). Side-Line previously covered the announcement of “Echoes of The End” in April 2026, when the album was confirmed as a digital deluxe edition and a physical 2CD via Alfa Matrix. Listen to “Choice”: Choice by Kant Kino About Kant Kino Kant Kino is a Norwegian electronic duo from Oslo, namely Lars Henrik Madsen and Kenneth Fredstie. The project formed after they wrote a tribute track for the ElektroStat festival, after which a Bunkertracks compilation appearance led to their Alfa Matrix signing. The duo’s debut album, “We Are Kant Kino – You Are Not”, appeared in 2010. It was followed by the “LRSBSS EP” on April 15, 2012, then the second full-length “Father Worked In Industry” on February 22, 2013. “Father Worked In Industry” was mixed and mastered by Claus Larsen of Leaether Strip. That release also produced the download singles “Just For The Comfort Of Sleep EP” on March 26, 2013 and “Ich Liebe Katarina Witt EP” on November 22, 2013. While working toward the third album, the band previewed new material with the teaser “Life” in February 2016. While working on a new album, they self-released the Motörhead/Kraftwerk hybrid “We Are The Roadcrew (Robots)” on December 16, 2016, ahead of “Kopfkino”, which was released on Alfa Matrix on January 13, 2017. In May 2017, Alfa Matrix built the first “Matrix:Reb00ted” volume around Kant Kino remixes. The duo later appeared on the Coldkill vs Kant Kino EP “Silent Morning” in 2018, released the Depeche Mode cover single “Pimpf and Touch Faith” in September 2019, and self-released “Enough! (Demo)” on June 30, 2022. Kenneth Fredstie in the meantime mastered “Face The Beat: Session 3” and Kant Kino contributed “Ich Liebe Katarina Witt (Video Edit)” and “Life (No Fucking Guitars Edit)” to the Face The Beat series. They also contributed a remix for Modulo One’s “No Way to Win”, and remixed the Side-Line charity single “Ukraina” in December 2022. In February 2026, Kant Kino returned with “Rodney: End-State Variations”, followed by the fourth album “Echoes Of The End”, reviewed above.
items._cn_summary: 挪威双人组合Kant Kino历经近九年沉淀后推出第四张专辑，核心仍为硬朗犀利的EBM，同时融入Electro-Pop旋律性与Future-Pop质感，并点缀早期Skinny Puppy式的暗黑工业氛围。专辑收录多达24首作品，以合成器复古质感为骨架，节奏紧凑且制作精良；人声表达有力而克制，与整体冷峻氛围契合。评论特别提及单曲"Choice"最具吸引力。部分段落对Assemblage 23的旋律手法有所借鉴，但整体仍保持EBM的强劲冲击力。发行厂牌Alfa Matrix为欧洲知名的暗潮/工业电子独立厂牌，乐评内容详实，涵盖乐队历史背景与作品脉络，属于原创乐评而非简单新闻转载。
